title: 7 · Research ethics and data rules
text: ~25 min · reading + quiz

title: 7 · Research ethics and data rules
text:
What you’ll learn

Why research has ethics rules, and the three principles behind them
What an IRB does
The data rules for our project, and the reasons for each
How credit works in research
How to use AI tools responsibly in research work

title: 7 · Research ethics and data rules
text:
1. Why research ethics exists
Research rules weren’t invented to slow people down. They were written after real harm was done.
The best-known U.S. example is the U.S. Public Health Service syphilis study at Tuskegee (1932–1972). Researchers followed hundreds of Black men with syphilis for decades without telling them their diagnosis, and kept treating them even after penicillin became the standard cure. When the study became public, the outrage led to new federal protections for research participants.
In 1979, a national commission published the Belmont Report. It sets out three principles that still guide U.S. research:








Principle
What it means
In everyday terms




Respect for persons
People decide for themselves whether to take part (informed consent). Extra protection goes to those who can’t fully decide.
Ask, explain and accept “no.”


Beneficence
Maximize benefits and minimize harms.
Don’t hurt people, and make the research worth doing.


Justice
Share the burdens and benefits of research fairly.
Don’t study only the people who are easiest to study, or leave out the people who would benefit.

title: 7 · Research ethics and data rules
text:
2. What an IRB does
An Institutional Review Board (IRB) is a committee at a university or hospital. It reviews research that involves people before the research starts. It checks that risks are low, consent is real, and private information is protected.
Not every project counts as “human subjects research.” Studying public streets, for example, isn’t the same as studying people. But universities still have rules for anyone who works on research, and some projects need training before you start. Your supervisor will tell you what’s required for your role.

title: 7 · Research ethics and data rules
text:
3. Our data rules, and why







Rule
Why




Never take screenshots, save, copy, download or print street images.
The images belong to the company that took them, and its terms limit storing them. We keep only an image id, never the picture.


Don’t try to work out where an image is.
Knowing the location could affect how you label (module 6), and locations can be sensitive.


Never describe a location in notes.
Same reasons. Notes should be about the labeling rules, not the place.


Never try to identify a person or vehicle you see in an image.
The people in street images didn’t agree to be studied. Respect for persons applies to them too.


Don’t share your login or let anyone else work under it.
Every label must be traceable to the person who made it, or the reliability checks in module 6 fall apart.


Don’t share project files outside the team. Don’t post about specific images or results online.
Results aren’t final until they’ve been checked and published. Sharing early can spread mistakes.


Don’t change settings or export data unless you’re asked to.
Settings and exports are part of the study record.



If something happens by accident (say, you took a screenshot without thinking), tell your supervisor. Delete it, and that’s the end of it. Honest mistakes reported quickly are easy to fix. Hidden ones aren’t.

title: 7 · Research ethics and data rules
text:
4. How credit works

Authorship on a scientific paper usually requires all four of these (the ICMJE criteria): a substantial contribution to the work, helping write or critically revise the paper, approving the final version, and agreeing to be accountable for it.
Acknowledgment recognizes people who helped in other ways, such as labeling data, checking records or reading papers. Volunteers are usually thanked by name, with permission.
Many journals now use the CRediT list of roles (such as data curation or investigation) to say exactly who did what.

If you’d like to work toward authorship, say so. Your supervisor can tell you what it would take.

title: 7 · Research ethics and data rules
text:
5. AI tools
AI tools such as chatbots can help you learn. For example, you could ask one to explain confounding a different way. But:

Never paste project materials, images, notes or data into an AI tool unless your supervisor has said that tool is approved for it.
AI makes things up, including fake references. Check anything it tells you against a real source.
If AI helped you with something you hand in, say so.

title: 7 · Research ethics and data rules
section: Why this matters for your work
text:
Why this matters for your work
These rules protect the people in the images, the project’s permission to use its data, and the credibility of the results. Following them is part of doing the work well.

title: 5 · Streets, design and safety
text: ~30 min · reading + quiz

title: 5 · Streets, design and safety
text:
What you’ll learn

Why speed matters more than almost anything else
Common street features that make walking safer
How strong the evidence is, and how to judge a study
Where our labeling checklist comes from

title: 5 · Streets, design and safety
text:
1. Speed and the human body
A study of U.S. crashes (Tefft, AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety, 2011) estimated a pedestrian’s risk of death by the speed of the car at impact:



Impact speed
Risk of death




23 mph
10%


32 mph
25%


42 mph
50%


50 mph
75%


58 mph
90%



Going from about 20 to about 40 mph doesn’t double the danger; it multiplies it several times. Speed also affects whether a crash happens at all: faster drivers need more distance to stop and see less of what’s beside the road.
That’s why so many safety designs work by slowing cars down where people walk.

title: 5 · Streets, design and safety
text:
2. Features that make walking safer
The U.S. Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) keeps a list of Proven Safety Countermeasures. Several are for people walking:








Feature
What it is
How it helps




High-visibility crosswalk
Bold bar markings, often with signs and lighting
Drivers see the crossing and the person in it


Pedestrian refuge island
A raised island in the middle of the street
People cross one direction of traffic at a time


Curb extension (bulb-out)
Sidewalk built out into the parking lane at a corner
Shorter crossing; people can see and be seen


Leading pedestrian interval
The walk signal starts a few seconds before cars get green
People are already in the crosswalk before turning cars arrive


Pedestrian hybrid beacon (HAWK)
An overhead signal that stops traffic only when a pedestrian pushes the button
A protected crossing on busy roads without a full signal


RRFB
Bright flashing yellow lights on a crossing sign
Draws drivers’ attention to a person waiting to cross


Road diet
Turning, for example, four lanes into two plus a center turn lane
Lower speeds and fewer lanes to cross


Lighting
Better street lighting at crossings
Most pedestrian deaths happen after dark (module 2)



FHWA reports, for example, that refuge islands reduce pedestrian crashes by about 32%, and pedestrian hybrid beacons by about 55%.

title: 5 · Streets, design and safety
text:
3. How strong is the evidence?
Not all studies are equally convincing. From weakest to strongest, roughly:

Cross-sectional: compare streets that have a feature with streets that don’t, at one point in time. This is the most open to confounding (module 4), because features aren’t placed at random.
Simple before–after: count crashes before and after a feature is installed. This is open to regression to the mean if the sites were chosen because they were bad.
Before–after with comparison sites: compare the change at treated sites with the change at similar untreated sites over the same years.
Before–after with empirical Bayes: like 3, plus a statistical correction for regression to the mean. This is the standard in road safety.

A famous example of why this matters: early studies found that marked crosswalks alone, with no other features, on wide, busy roads were linked with more pedestrian crashes than unmarked crossings. Paint alone may not be enough on fast multi-lane roads. The usual advice is to add other features, such as refuge islands or beacons, there. (Zegeer et al., FHWA, 2005)

title: 5 · Streets, design and safety
text:
4. Where our checklist comes from
To measure streets consistently, researchers use audit tools: checklists of street features with exact definitions. Our labeling classes descend from an audit tool called CANVAS, adapted for images. Because related projects share this ancestry, their checklists aren’t fully independent measures. That matters when comparing results across studies.

title: 5 · Streets, design and safety
section: Why this matters for your work
text:
Why this matters for your work
Most of the classes you’ll label (crosswalks, medians and refuge islands, curb extensions, signals, beacons, lane markings) are on the list above. Your labels let researchers ask whether these features are linked to fewer crashes across a whole city, not just at a few sites.

title: 3 · Where crash data come from
text:
What you’ll learn

The main sources of crash and injury data
How injury severity is recorded
What these data sources miss
Why studying one street is harder than it looks

title: 3 · Where crash data come from
text:
1. Police crash reports
Most crash data start with a police report. An officer at the scene fills in a form: date, time, location, the people and vehicles involved, road and weather conditions, and how badly people seem to be hurt. States collect these reports into databases.
Police reports are the most complete source on where crashes happen, which makes them central to street-level research. But they’re filled in quickly, at the scene, by people who aren’t doctors.

title: 3 · Where crash data come from
text:
2. National databases








Source
What it covers
Run by




FARS (Fatality Analysis Reporting System)
Every crash on a public road in which someone died within 30 days. National data back to 1975.
NHTSA


CRSS (Crash Report Sampling System)
A national sample of police reports of all severities, used to estimate totals
NHTSA


NEISS (National Electronic Injury Surveillance System)
A sample of about 100 hospital emergency departments, used to estimate injuries nationally
U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission


Hospital and trauma registries
Detailed medical information on people treated
States and hospitals

title: 3 · Where crash data come from
text:
3. How severity is recorded: KABCO
Police usually record injuries on the KABCO scale:



Code
Meaning




K
Killed


A
Suspected serious injury


B
Suspected minor injury


C
Possible injury


O
No apparent injury



Researchers often combine K and A into KSI: killed or seriously injured.

title: 3 · Where crash data come from
text:
4. What the data miss

Underreporting. Many crashes involving people walking or cycling, especially minor ones, never reach a police report. The person may go home, or straight to a hospital.
Severity guesses. An officer’s “A” or “B” at the scene can differ from what doctors later find.
Location errors. The location may be recorded at the nearest intersection, or not exactly.
Missing exposure. Crash data say nothing about how many people walked safely past the same spot (module 4).

Linking police reports to hospital records helps fill these gaps, but it’s hard to do.

title: 3 · Where crash data come from
section: 5. Why one street is hard to study
text:
5. Why one street is hard to study
Fatal crashes are, thankfully, rare on any single street. A block might have zero deaths for ten years, then one. Was the street dangerous, or unlucky? You can’t tell from one block.
That’s why researchers:

use KSI, or all injury crashes, not just deaths, to get more events;
study many streets at once, and compare streets with and without a feature;
use statistical methods that account for chance (module 4, regression to the mean).







NoteGo deeper (college)






FARS counts deaths within 30 days of the crash; other systems define deaths differently.
CRSS and NEISS are samples, so their national totals are estimates with uncertainty. FARS is a census.
Crash counts per street segment are usually modeled with negative binomial regression. Counts vary more than a simple Poisson model expects.

title: 3 · Where crash data come from
section: Why this matters for your work
text:
Why this matters for your work
Crash data tell us where people were hurt. Your labels tell us what the street looked like. The study needs both, linked carefully.

title: 1 · Public health in one hour
text: ~40 min · reading + quiz

title: 1 · Public health in one hour
text:
What you’ll learn

How public health differs from medicine
The three levels of prevention
Why injuries aren’t “accidents,” and the tool researchers use to study them (the Haddon matrix)
The Safe System approach to road safety
Why changing the environment often works better than telling people to be careful

title: 1 · Public health in one hour
text:
1. Populations, not just patients
A doctor treats the person in front of them. Public health asks why so many people are getting sick or hurt in the first place, and what would protect everyone at once.

Medicine: “This patient was struck by a car. Let’s treat the broken leg.”
Public health: “Twenty people were struck on this street this year. What about the street is causing that, and what would prevent the next twenty?”

Public health’s biggest successes came mostly from changes that protect everyone, not from treating individuals one at a time: clean water, vaccines, smoke-free laws, seat belts and safer cars.

title: 1 · Public health in one hour
text:
2. Three levels of prevention








Level
Goal
Road safety example




Primary
Stop the event from happening
Lower speeds and a refuge island so people can cross in two stages


Secondary
Reduce harm when it happens
Car fronts designed to be less deadly to people on foot; lower impact speeds


Tertiary
Reduce the long-term damage afterward
Fast ambulance response, trauma care, rehabilitation



Most of our project is about primary prevention: finding street features linked to fewer crashes.

title: 1 · Public health in one hour
text:
3. Injuries are not accidents
“Accident” suggests bad luck that nobody could have predicted. But injuries follow patterns. They happen more on certain streets, at certain times and to certain people, which means they can be predicted and prevented. That’s why many agencies now say “crash,” not “accident.”
In the 1960s, William Haddon Jr., a physician and engineer, created a simple grid for thinking about any injury. It’s called the Haddon matrix:










Person
Vehicle
Environment




Before the crash
Walking at night in dark clothing; alcohol
Driver’s view blocked by a tall hood; distraction
No crosswalk; long gap between crossings; poor lighting; high speed limit


During the crash
Older age, so the body is more fragile
Impact speed; front-end shape
Hard objects nearby


After the crash
Health before the crash
Hit-and-run
Distance to a trauma center; ambulance access



Notice how many boxes involve the vehicle and environment, not just the person walking. Every box is a place where prevention could work.

title: 1 · Public health in one hour
text:
4. The Safe System approach
Traditional road safety often focused on changing behavior (“look both ways,” “don’t jaywalk”). The Safe System approach, adopted in the U.S. National Roadway Safety Strategy (2022), starts from different ideas:

Deaths and serious injuries are unacceptable.
People make mistakes. The road system should allow for them.
Human bodies are fragile. There are limits to the crash forces we can survive.
Responsibility is shared among road designers, vehicle makers, drivers, people walking, and policymakers.
Safety should be proactive. Find and fix risks before crashes happen, not only after.
Redundancy matters. If one layer of protection fails, others should still work.

Vision Zero, adopted by many cities including Philadelphia, applies the same thinking with a goal of zero traffic deaths.

title: 1 · Public health in one hour
section: 5. Change the environment, not just the person
text:
5. Change the environment, not just the person
Public health leaders often describe a “health impact pyramid” (Frieden, 2010). Education and counseling sit at the top: they matter, but each person has to change their behavior, every time. At the base are changes that make the safe choice the default, so they protect people without anyone having to do anything.
For walking safety:

Top of the pyramid: a campaign telling people to wear bright clothes at night.
Base of the pyramid: street lighting, slower street designs and safe places to cross.

Both have a role, but the base usually reaches more people and lasts longer. That’s why our project studies streets, not walkers’ behavior.

title: 1 · Public health in one hour
section: Why this matters for your work
text:
Why this matters for your work
The features you label, such as crosswalks, medians, signals and curb ramps, are the environment column of the Haddon matrix and the base of the pyramid. They’re the things a city can actually change.

title: Glossary
text:
Plain-language definitions. Use the search box to jump to a term.







Term
Meaning




Confounder
Something linked to both the feature being studied and the outcome, which can create a false association. Example: foot traffic, which is linked to both crosswalks and crashes.


Count
The number of events, like crashes, without dividing by anything.


Denominator
The number you divide by to turn a count into a rate, such as people, walkers or miles walked.


Ecological fallacy
Wrongly concluding something about individuals from data about areas.


Empirical Bayes (EB)
A statistical method that pulls very high or low crash counts toward what’s typical for similar streets, to reduce regression to the mean.


Epidemiology
The study of how health problems are distributed in populations, and what causes them.


Exposure
How much people are at risk. For pedestrians: how many walk, how far, and how much traffic they meet.


FARS
Fatality Analysis Reporting System: the U.S. national database of fatal crashes.


HAWK / PHB
Pedestrian hybrid beacon: an overhead signal that stays dark until a pedestrian pushes a button.


HIN
High-injury network: the small share of a city’s streets where most serious crashes happen.


Inter-rater reliability
How well two or more labelers agree when they label the same things independently.


IoU
Intersection over union: how much two drawn boxes overlap, from 0 (none) to 1 (identical).


IRB
Institutional Review Board: the committee that reviews research involving people to protect them.


Kappa (κ)
A measure of agreement between raters that removes the agreement expected by chance.


KABCO
The police scale of injury severity: K = killed, A = serious, B = minor, C = possible, O = none.


KSI
Killed or seriously injured (K + A on the KABCO scale).


Rate
A count divided by a denominator, such as crashes per 1,000 walkers.


Regression to the mean
The tendency of unusually high or low values to be closer to average next time, by chance alone.


Reliability
Consistency: getting the same answer each time.


RRFB
Rectangular rapid-flashing beacon: yellow flashing lights on a pedestrian crossing sign.


Safe System
An approach to road safety that assumes people will make mistakes and designs roads so that mistakes aren’t fatal.


Validity
Accuracy: measuring what you mean to measure.


Vision Zero
A goal and strategy of zero traffic deaths and serious injuries.


ZAT
A transport analysis zone in Bogotá (zona de análisis de transporte), used for area-level analysis.

title: 0 · Welcome: how the project fits together
text:
The problem
In 2023, 7,314 people were killed while walking in the United States, about one every 72 minutes, and about 68,000 more were injured (NHTSA). Most of these deaths can be prevented. They don’t happen at random. They cluster on certain kinds of streets, at certain times, and among certain groups of people. Older adults are hit especially hard: as we age we walk more slowly, see less well at night, and are more likely to die from an injury that a younger person would survive.
When something is common, serious and preventable, it’s a public health problem, not just bad luck.

title: 0 · Welcome: how the project fits together
text:
What our project does
WalkSafe-AI is a research project funded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health (National Institute on Aging). We ask one question:

Which features of a street make walking more or less dangerous, and can we measure those features across a whole city?

Sending people to walk every street with a clipboard (a “street audit”) works, but it’s slow and expensive. So we’re testing whether computers can do part of the job by “reading” street-level photos. They would look for things like crosswalks, sidewalks, traffic lights, medians and curb ramps.
For a computer to learn this, and for us to check whether it got it right, people have to label images carefully first. That’s often where volunteers come in.

title: 0 · Welcome: how the project fits together
text:
Where your work fits
 Street images      People label         Computer models     We compare labels     Link street features
 (we never keep  ->  what they see   ->   learn to find   ->  from people and   ->  to crash data, with
  copies)            (you!)               the same things     models                careful statistics
Each step depends on the one before it. If the labels are inconsistent, everything after them is weaker. Careful, consistent labeling is real scientific work.

title: 0 · Welcome: how the project fits together
text:
Where things stand
We try to be accurate about what’s finished and what isn’t:

Bogotá, Colombia: demonstrated. Earlier published work measured 27 street features from images across the city and linked them to crashes.
Philadelphia: an early prototype, plus one completed study testing how well computer-made measurements match crash patterns.
Planned tools (for example, tools to help cities choose where to invest) are not built yet.

If you describe the project to anyone (friends, teachers, college applications), use this wording. Please don’t say it does more than it does.

Ask when unsure. Write down what confused you (for labeling, the tile id) and ask your supervisor.
Protect the data. Module 7 explains the rules, such as never taking screenshots of images.
Be honest about your time. Tell us if you get busy. It’s much better than rushing.

title: 2 · Who gets hurt walking, and why
text:
What you’ll learn

How many people are killed and hurt while walking, in the U.S. and worldwide
Where and when it happens
Why older adults are a focus of our project
Why risk isn’t shared equally

title: 2 · Who gets hurt walking, and why
text:
1. The numbers
United States, 2023 (NHTSA, Traffic Safety Facts: Pedestrians, 2023 Data):

7,314 people were killed while walking. That’s about one every 72 minutes.
About 68,000 more were injured.
People walking were 18% of everyone killed in traffic, up from 15% in 2014.
Pedestrian deaths rose from 4,910 in 2014 to a peak of 7,593 in 2022, even though cars got safer for the people inside them.

Worldwide (WHO, Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023):

About 1.19 million people die in road crashes each year.
About 23% of them, roughly 274,000 people, were walking.
Between 2010 and 2021, total road deaths fell slightly, but pedestrian deaths rose by about 3%.

title: 2 · Who gets hurt walking, and why
text:
2. Where and when
From the same 2023 U.S. data:



Fact
Share of pedestrian deaths




In urban areas
84%


Not at an intersection (mid-block, along roads)
74%


In the dark
77%


Hit-and-run
24%


Male
70%



Two patterns stand out. Most deaths happen away from intersections, often where there’s no safe place to cross nearby. And most happen after dark, when drivers see less and often drive faster.

title: 2 · Who gets hurt walking, and why
text:
3. Older adults
Our project is funded by the National Institute on Aging, so older adults (we use 60 and over, following the World Health Organization) are a focus.

In 2023, people 60 and over were about 24% of the U.S. population but about 30% of pedestrian deaths.
Their death rate was 2.7 per 100,000 people, compared with 2.0 for people under 60.

Why?

Frailty: the same impact is more likely to kill an older person.
Walking speed: many crossing signals are timed for faster walkers.
Vision and hearing: these can make it harder to judge gaps in traffic, especially at night.
Aging in place: many older adults want to keep living independently, and walking is how many of them get groceries, see friends and stay active. Unsafe streets can mean staying home, which harms health in other ways.







NoteSaying it accurately



Older adults are over-represented among pedestrian deaths. But in 2023 the highest rates by age group were among adults in their 40s to early 60s. Don’t say older adults have “the highest rate of any age group.” It isn’t true, and getting details right is part of being trusted.

title: 2 · Who gets hurt walking, and why
text:
4. Risk isn’t shared equally
A 2025 review of U.S. research (Dumbaugh and Stiles) found that, per person:

Lower-income areas have about 3 times as many pedestrian deaths as wealthier areas.
Compared with White non-Hispanic people, Hispanic people are about 1.6 times, Black people about 1.7 times, and American Indian and Alaska Native people about 4 times as likely to be killed while walking.

The same review found little support for the usual explanations, such as “they just walk more” or drinking. The biggest difference was why people walk:

Wealthier households walk mostly for leisure. If a street feels unsafe, they can walk somewhere else, or drive.
Lower-income households walk mostly because they have to: to work, school, shops and the bus. They can’t avoid dangerous streets.
Road design and investment make it worse. Wide, fast roads with few safe crossings often run through lower-income neighborhoods.

This is a health equity issue: avoidable, unfair differences in health between groups.

title: 2 · Who gets hurt walking, and why
text:
5. Beyond the U.S.
In many cities in Latin America, Africa and Asia, people walking make up a larger share of road deaths than in the U.S. Part of our team’s earlier work was in Bogotá, Colombia. There, researchers measured street features from images across the whole city and linked them to crashes.






NoteGo deeper (college)






Rates depend on the denominator (module 4). Per-population rates, like those above, don’t account for how much each group walks. Per-trip or per-mile rates can tell a different story.
U.S. vehicles have grown larger and taller. An Insurance Institute for Highway Safety study of about 18,000 crashes (Hu, Monfort and Cicchino, 2024) found that vehicles with tall, blunt front ends were linked with about 44% higher pedestrian fatality risk than vehicles with low, sloped fronts.
Look up the NHTSA fact sheet yourself and find the table by age and sex. Which group has the highest rate?

title: 2 · Who gets hurt walking, and why
section: Why this matters for your work
text:
Why this matters for your work
Most deaths happen mid-block, at night, on urban arterials. When you label sidewalks, crossings, medians and signals, you’re measuring exactly the features that may make those places safer.

title: 4 · Thinking like an epidemiologist
text: ~40 min · reading + worked examples + quiz

title: 4 · Thinking like an epidemiologist
text:
What you’ll learn

Why counts can mislead, and why we use rates
What exposure means, and why it’s the biggest trap in pedestrian safety research
What confounding is, with a worked example
Two more traps: the ecological fallacy and regression to the mean

All the examples use Riverton, a made-up town. The numbers are invented to make the ideas clear.

title: 4 · Thinking like an epidemiologist
text:
1. Counts vs. rates
Riverton has two neighborhoods:




Pedestrian crashes per year
People crossing streets per day




Northside
40
20,000


Southside
10
2,000



Which neighborhood is more dangerous to walk in?
Northside has four times as many crashes. But it also has ten times as many people walking. Divide crashes by walkers:

Northside: 40 ÷ 20,000 = 2 crashes per 1,000 daily walkers
Southside: 10 ÷ 2,000 = 5 crashes per 1,000 daily walkers

For each person walking, Southside is 2.5 times more dangerous.
A count tells you where crashes pile up. A rate tells you how risky it is for each person. The number you divide by is called the denominator. Choosing it is one of the most important decisions in epidemiology.

title: 4 · Thinking like an epidemiologist
text:
2. Exposure: the central trap
Exposure is how much people are “at risk” of the outcome. For pedestrian crashes, that means how many people walk, how far, and how many cars pass them.
Busy places have more crashes partly because they are busy. More people walking near more cars means more chances for a crash, even if the street is no more dangerous per person.
This matters because cities put safety features where people and traffic are. Crosswalks, walk signals and curb ramps go on busy streets. So if you just count crashes, safety features can look dangerous.

title: 4 · Thinking like an epidemiologist
text:
3. Confounding: a worked example
Riverton has 1,000 intersections. Some have marked crosswalks; some don’t. Here are crashes per intersection per year:
Ignoring foot traffic:




Intersections
Crashes per intersection




Crosswalk
500
1.7


No crosswalk
500
0.8



Crosswalks look terrible: more than twice as many crashes! Should Riverton remove them?
Now split by how busy the intersection is:









Crosswalk
No crosswalk




Quiet intersections
100 intersections, 0.5 crashes each
400 intersections, 0.5 crashes each


Busy intersections
400 intersections, 2.0 crashes each
100 intersections, 2.0 crashes each



Within quiet intersections, crosswalks make no difference. The same is true within busy ones. The first table looked bad only because most crosswalks are at busy intersections, and busy intersections have more crashes for every kind of street.
Foot and car traffic here is a confounder. It’s linked both to the thing we’re studying (crosswalks) and to the outcome (crashes), so it creates a false association.






ImportantThe rule we follow



Any study linking street features to crashes must account for exposure (how many people walk and how much traffic there is). Otherwise the results can point in the wrong direction.








NoteGo deeper (college)






Check the arithmetic: crosswalk average = (100 × 0.5 + 400 × 2.0) / 500 = 1.7. The crude ratio is 1.7 / 0.8 ≈ 2.1, and the ratio within each group is 1.0.
In real studies, exposure is rarely measured well. Pedestrian counts exist for only a few locations, so researchers model them. That leaves residual confounding: some bias stays even after adjustment.
Researchers draw directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to decide which variables to adjust for. Here: traffic → crosswalk, traffic → crashes, and crosswalk → crashes (the effect we want). Adjusting for traffic blocks the “back door” path.
Adjusting for the wrong thing can cause bias too. For example, don’t adjust for something that the street feature itself changes.

title: 4 · Thinking like an epidemiologist
text:
4. The ecological fallacy
Suppose Riverton’s zones with more bus stops have more pedestrian crashes. Does that mean people who use buses are at higher risk?
Not necessarily. The data describe areas, not people. Maybe the crashes in bus-heavy zones happen to people who never ride buses. Jumping from an area-level pattern to a claim about individuals is called the ecological fallacy.
Area-level (“ecological”) studies are useful: cities make decisions about areas. Just describe the findings as being about places, not persons.

title: 4 · Thinking like an epidemiologist
text:
5. Regression to the mean
Riverton picks the 10 intersections with the most crashes last year and paints new crosswalks there. Next year, crashes at those 10 drop by 30%. Did the paint work?
Maybe. But crash counts bounce around from year to year by chance. An intersection that had an unusually bad year is likely to have a more ordinary year next, even with no change at all. This is regression to the mean, and it makes treatments placed at “the worst spots” look better than they are.
Researchers handle this with comparison sites and with statistical methods that pull extreme counts toward what’s typical for similar streets. One such method is called empirical Bayes.

title: 4 · Thinking like an epidemiologist
section: Why this matters for your work
text:
Why this matters for your work

If you’re labeling images, you’ll often see that busy streets have more of everything: more crosswalks, more signals, more signs. That’s expected, and it’s exactly why the analysis has to adjust for exposure. Label what you see, and leave the interpretation to the analysis.
If you’re reading papers, ask of each one: Did they account for exposure? Are they talking about places or people? Did they choose sites because they were extreme?

title: 6 · Measuring streets from images
text: ~35 min · reading + quiz

title: 6 · Measuring streets from images
text:
What you’ll learn

The difference between validity and reliability
Why we have two or more people label the same images
Why the rules say “label only what you see”
Why we keep labelers blind to each other’s work, and freeze labels before comparing
How mistakes in labels can (or can’t) bias a study

title: 6 · Measuring streets from images
text:
1. Ways to measure a street









Method
How
Good
Not so good




Field audit
A trained person walks the street with a checklist
Sees everything up close
Slow, costly, hard to cover a whole city


Virtual audit
A person looks at street-level images on a computer
Faster, no travel
Images may be old; some things are hidden


Computer vision
A model finds features in images automatically
Can cover a whole city
Makes its own kinds of mistakes, and must be checked against people



Our project uses virtual audits by people to teach and check computer models. Many checklists in this field, including ours, descend from the same audit tool (CANVAS), so they aren’t fully independent of each other.

title: 6 · Measuring streets from images
text:
2. Validity and reliability
Think of a dartboard:

Valid means hitting the bullseye: measuring what you mean to measure.
Reliable means hitting the same spot every time: consistent, even if it’s off-center.

A measurement can be reliable but not valid (always off in the same way), but it can’t be valid without being reliable. If two people label the same image differently, at least one is wrong, and we can’t tell which.
That’s why consistency comes first. A clear, shared rule applied the same way by everyone beats each person’s private idea of what’s “right.”

title: 6 · Measuring streets from images
section: 3. Why two people label the same images
text:
3. Why two people label the same images
We have two (sometimes three) people independently label some of the same images. Then we measure how often they agree. This is called inter-rater reliability.
But agreement can happen by luck. If 90% of images have no bike lane, two people who both always click “no bike lane” agree 90% of the time without even looking. So researchers use statistics like Cohen’s kappa (κ), which measures agreement beyond what chance would give:

κ = 0: no better than chance
κ = 1: perfect agreement
Roughly 0.6 or above is often called “substantial”

For boxes drawn around objects, we also check whether two boxes overlap enough to count as the same object. The usual measure is called IoU (intersection over union).
Human–human agreement also gives us a benchmark for the computer. If two trained people agree only so often, we can’t expect a model to do better than that.

title: 6 · Measuring streets from images
text:
4. “Label only what you see”
You’ll see this rule a lot. It means:

Label what’s visible in this image, not what “a street like this usually has.”
If you can’t tell what something is, don’t label it, or flag it as unsure if the rules allow.
Don’t use outside knowledge, like “I know there’s a crosswalk at that corner.”

Why so strict? If labelers fill in what they expect, the labels start to reflect their assumptions, and different people have different assumptions. Then the labels measure the labelers, not the street.

title: 6 · Measuring streets from images
text:
5. Blinding and freezing

Blind: labelers don’t see each other’s labels, and don’t discuss specific images until the comparison is done. If you talk it over first, your agreement no longer tells us how consistent the rules are. It only shows that you talked.
Freeze: when everyone finishes, the labels are locked (saved with a digital fingerprint) before anyone compares them. Then nobody can, even by accident, “fix” labels after seeing the results.
Written rules first: the rules and the analysis plan are written down and signed before the data are examined. If the plan changes, the change is written down too, with the reason.

None of this is about distrust. It’s how science protects itself from its own wishful thinking. The same habits are used in clinical trials.

title: 6 · Measuring streets from images
text:
6. When do labeling mistakes matter?
Everyone makes mistakes. What matters is the pattern:

Random mistakes, made about as often everywhere, usually make real patterns look weaker than they are. That’s annoying, but it’s a known problem.
Mistakes that differ by place are more dangerous. Suppose labelers miss crosswalks more often on dark, low-quality images, and those come mostly from poorer neighborhoods. Then the data can create a pattern that isn’t real.

That’s one reason we sample images from many kinds of neighborhoods. It’s also why the rules ask you to flag images that won’t load or that you can’t read, instead of guessing.






NoteGo deeper (college)






Random error in an exposure is called non-differential misclassification. With two categories it usually biases associations toward the null. Error that differs by outcome or by group is differential, and it can bias in either direction.
Kappa depends on how common the feature is (the prevalence paradox). Rare features can have high raw agreement but low κ. Report both.
Reliability sets an upper limit on validity. The correlation between a measure and anything else is capped by how reliable the measure is.
Search for “pre-registration” and “researcher degrees of freedom” to see why signed plans matter.

title: 6 · Measuring streets from images
section: Why this matters for your work
text:
Why this matters for your work

Consistency beats cleverness. Follow the written definitions exactly, even when you’d draw the line elsewhere.
Ask, don’t guess. Note the image id and ask your supervisor. The answer goes to every labeler, so the rules stay shared.
Don’t compare notes on specific images with other labelers until your supervisor says the comparison is done.
Take your time, and stop when you’re tired. Tired labeling is inconsistent labeling. Submit or close the page when you take a break.

title: 8 · From research to safer streets
text:
What you’ll learn

Who uses pedestrian safety research, and how
How to read a safety map or dashboard carefully
Why the words we use matter
Careers in injury prevention and transportation safety

title: 8 · From research to safer streets
text:
1. Who uses this research







Who
What they do with it




City transportation departments
Decide which streets to redesign first, and which features to use


Vision Zero programs
Map the “high-injury network,” the small share of streets with most serious crashes, and track progress


State departments of transportation
Fund safety projects; set design standards for state roads, which are often the most dangerous urban streets


Health departments
Treat traffic injury as a public health problem; link it to physical activity, aging and equity


Advocates and community groups
Push for changes on their own streets, using data as evidence


Researchers
Test which features actually work, and for whom



Research rarely changes a street by itself. It becomes one piece of evidence that planners, residents and elected officials weigh along with cost, space and what the community wants.

title: 8 · From research to safer streets
text:
2. Reading maps and dashboards carefully
Maps of crashes are powerful, and easy to misread. Use what you learned in module 4:

Counts or rates? A map of crash counts mostly shows where people and cars are.
Exposure: busy downtown streets will always look “red” on a count map.
Places, not people: an area-level map describes places, not individuals (the ecological fallacy).
Time period: a few years of data can be noisy. Was the period chosen because it was unusual?
What’s not built yet: a research dashboard may show early results. Read its notes about what’s demonstrated and what’s still a prototype.

title: 8 · From research to safer streets
text:
3. Words matter
The words we use shape who gets blamed, and what gets fixed.








Instead of
Try
Why




“Accident”
“Crash”
Crashes are predictable and preventable (module 1)


“Pedestrian was hit by a car”
“A driver struck a person walking”
Names who was involved, not just the object


“Jaywalker”
“Person crossing mid-block”
Most deaths happen mid-block, often where no safe crossing is nearby (module 2)


“Pedestrian error”
Describe the street: “no crossing for half a mile”
Points to what can be changed



Accurate language also means not overstating results. Say “linked with” rather than “causes” unless the study design supports a causal claim.

title: 8 · From research to safer streets
text:
4. Careers
People who work on this problem include:

Epidemiologists and biostatisticians at universities, health departments and the CDC’s injury prevention programs
Transportation engineers and planners at city and state departments of transportation
Data scientists building tools like the ones in this project
Policy analysts and advocates at nonprofits and government agencies
Emergency medicine and trauma professionals who treat injuries and study prevention

Useful college majors include public health, epidemiology, statistics, data science, civil engineering, urban planning, geography and computer science. Many of these fields welcome people from the others.
